plain_english:
Should we destroy this thief and this cheater? No, don't say that. Say this instead: This person is confused and mistaken about the most important things. He's blind — not physically blind, but blind to what's good and what's bad. Should we destroy him? If you put it that way, you'll see how cruel that sounds. It's like saying we should destroy someone who can't see or hear.

The worst loss is losing the most important things. The most important thing in every person is their ability to choose well. When someone has lost that ability, why are you angry at them? You shouldn't let another person's bad choices upset you. Feel sorry for them instead. Stop being so quick to take offense and hate. Stop saying things like "These awful, disgusting people." When did you suddenly become so wise? And why are you so irritable?
original_excerpt: Ought not then this robber and this adulterer to be destroyed? By no means say so, but speak rather in this way: This man who has been mistaken and deceived about the most important things, and blinded, not in the faculty of vision which distinguishes white and black, but in the faculty which distinguishes good and bad, should we not destroy him? If you speak thus you will see how inhuman this is which you say, and that it is just as if you would say, Ought we not to destroy this blind and deaf man? But if the greatest harm is the privation of the greatest things, and the greatest thing in every man is the will or choice such as it ought to be, and a man is deprived of this will, why are you also angry with him? Man, you ought not to be affected contrary to nature by the bad things of another. Pity him rather; drop this readiness to be offended and to hate, and these words which the many utter: "These accursed and odious fellows." How have you been made so wise at once? and how are you so peevish?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with the Errors (faults) of Others

plain_english: Why do we get angry? Because we value the things that others take from us. Don't admire your clothes, and you won't be angry at the thief. Think about it this way: you have nice clothes and your neighbor doesn't. You have a window and you want to air out your clothes. The thief doesn't know what makes life truly good. He thinks it's having nice clothes — the same thing you think. So of course he's going to come take them. When you show cake to hungry people and then eat it all yourself, do you really expect them not to grab it from you? Don't provoke them. Don't have a window. Don't air your clothes. I recently had an iron lamp next to my household shrine. I heard noise at the door, ran down, and found the lamp was gone. I thought about it: the person who took it did nothing unusual. So what's my response? Tomorrow, I told myself, you'll get a clay lamp. You can only lose what you have. "I lost my coat." That's because you had a coat. "My head hurts." Do your horns hurt? Why are you upset about that? We only lose things we possess. We only feel pain about things we have.
original_excerpt: Why then are we angry? Is it because we value so much the things of which these men rob us? Do not admire your clothes, and then you will not be angry with the thief. Consider this matter thus: you have fine clothes; your neighbor has not; you have a window; you wish to air the clothes. The thief does not know wherein man's good consists, but he thinks that it consist in having fine clothes, the very thing which you also think. Must he not then come and take them away? When you show a cake to greedy persons, and swallow it all yourself, do you expect them not to snatch it from you? Do not provoke them; do not have a window; do not air your clothes. I also lately had an iron lamp placed by the side of my household gods; hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp; for a man only loses that which he has. I have lost my garment. The reason is that you had a garment. I have a pain in my head. Have you any pain in your horns? Why then are you troubled? For we only lose those things, we have only pains about those things, which we possess.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with the Errors (faults) of Others

plain_english: But the tyrant will chain—what? Your leg. He will take away—what? Your head. What then can he not chain and not take away? Your will. This is why the ancients taught: Know yourself. So we should practice with small things first, then move to bigger ones. Your head hurts. Don't say, "Poor me!" Your ear hurts. Don't say "Poor me!" I'm not saying you can't groan out loud, but don't groan on the inside. And if your servant is slow bringing you a bandage, don't cry out and torture yourself and say, "Everyone hates me." Who wouldn't hate someone like that? From now on, rely on these ideas. Walk upright and free. Don't trust in your physical size like an athlete does. You shouldn't be invincible the way a donkey is.
original_excerpt: But the tyrant will chain—what? The leg. He will take away—what? The neck. What then will he not chain and not take away? The will. This is why the ancients taught the maxim, Know thyself. Therefore we ought to exercise ourselves in small things, and beginning with them to proceed to the greater. I have pain in the head. Do not say, Alas! I have pain in the ear. Do not say alas! And I do not say that you are not allowed to groan, but do not groan inwardly; and if your slave is slow in bringing a bandage, do not cry out and torment yourself, and say, Every body hates me; for who would not hate such a man? For the future, relying on these opinions, walk about upright, free; not trusting to the size of your body, as an athlete, for a man ought not to be invincible in the way that an ass is.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with the Errors (faults) of Others
